演奏馬頭琴時，琴身近直立，音箱置於腿上或兩腿間；中文資料亦記席地而坐，將音箱左下: When playing the morin khuur the body is held nearly upright, the soundbox resting on the leg or between the legs; Chinese sources also describe sitting on the ground with the lower left corner of the soundbox gripped between the knees. The right hand holds the horsehair bow from below, and gripping it backhand lets the hair be tightened or slackened. Sound comes from the hair rubbing the two strings, and double stops and harmonics are possible. The strings are not pressed from the front: the index and middle fingers push them from left to right with the base of the nail, and the ring and little fingers push with the fingertips; when the little finger cannot reach the inner string, it can come in under the outer string to push it. A beginner practises scales and trains the ear so that the fingers correct the pitch by themselves; the point is the pressure of the fingers, the weight of the bow and a steady volume after each bow change, aiming for a clear note with steady volume and pitch.

馬頭琴屬弦鳴樂器，發聲體為兩束琴弦，傳統以公馬或母馬尾毛製成，現代亦用尼龍弦；琴: The morin khuur is a chordophone whose sounding body is two pairs of strings, traditionally of stallion's or mare's tail hair, with nylon strings also used today; the bow is strung with horsehair and rubbed with larch or cedar resin. The frame of the body is mostly wood, the soundbox is covered with horse, sheep or camel hide, and all-wood soundboxes also exist; the soundboard is usually pine or spruce and the back and sides mostly birch, with maple on some classical instruments. The tuning pegs are traditionally ebony or rosewood; the materials of the other parts are not recorded.
馬頭琴為傳統蒙古弓弦樂器，祖先為馬尾胡琴，由唐宋時期胡琴發展而成，成吉思汗時已流: The morin khuur is the traditional bowed string instrument of Mongolia. Its ancestor is the horsehair huqin, which developed from the huqin of the Tang and Song periods; it was already current among the people in the time of Genghis Khan, and it is played by Mongols in Mongolia and in Inner Mongolia, Liaoning, Jilin, Heilongjiang, Gansu and Xinjiang in China. The earliest record of the name morin khuur dates from 1907. After the twentieth century, Qi Baoligao reformed the instrument from 1973 on, enlarging its volume and range, switching to a white pine soundboard in 1996, and absorbing techniques from the violin, erhu, sihu and cello; in 1986 he formed an ensemble, in 1989 the Chinese Morin Khuur Society was founded, and in 2001 a thousand players performed Ten Thousand Galloping Horses. All-wood soundboxes appeared from the 1970s, and the instrument is listed as a UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage masterpiece.

馬頭琴為弦鳴弓弦樂器，發音來自兩條馬尾或尼龍弦經木橋傳至梯形音箱。標準定音多為降: The morin khuur is a bowed chordophone: two horsehair or nylon strings pass over a wooden bridge into a trapezoidal soundbox. The standard tuning is usually B-flat and F; the F string can play from F to F', and the B-flat string has further harmonics such as B-flat', F" and B". The player holds the bow from below in the right hand and can tighten the horsehair, controlling timbre and volume; a clear note depends on finger pressure, bow weight and steadiness across bow changes. Instruments from central Mongolia are larger and louder, those from Inner Mongolia smaller. The bow runs outside the strings and the strings are pushed with the base of the nail, so double stops and harmonics are possible; the timbre is rounder and more low-lying than other bowed instruments, and the volume weaker.
馬頭琴為蒙古傳統弓弦樂器，來源記載其可用於獨奏、與四胡等樂器合奏，以及民歌、說書: The morin khuur is the traditional bowed string instrument of Mongolia; the source records that it can play solo, join ensembles with the sihu and other instruments, and accompany folk songs and storytelling, and that it can also play Western classical music and Mongolian-style repertoire. Players often use trills in thirds and fourths to imitate singing, and imitate the neighing of a horse. The source also mentions that Qi Baoligao once led a thousand morin khuur players in Ten Thousand Galloping Horses, which shows that the instrument can take part in large-scale national instrumental ensembles.
